What is real here: every index on this page was built from our 1,076 caption chunks of Caltech CS 156 (18 lectures) and their bge-m3 vectors. Recall is measured against exact search; speed is this Mac, one CPU thread, on a tiny corpus. The three questions and their answer marks are ours. Building blocks of retrieval · a layered lesson

Indexing for RAG

A retriever must find the few chunks that answer a question among thousands or millions, fast. The data structure that makes this fast is the index. This page explains the common kinds four times over: as a picture, for a student, with the research, and as the decision in our thesis. Every index you can touch here is real and built from our own lecture chunks.

TL;DR

  • Two families. A keyword index (inverted index, scored with BM25) maps each word to the chunks that contain it. A vector index stores one embedding per chunk and finds the nearest vectors to the question. Learned sparse (SPLADE, the sparse output of bge-m3) puts learned word weights into an inverted index; multi-vector (ColBERT) keeps one vector per token.
  • Exact (flat) vector search compares the question with every vector. It is always right and costs N comparisons. Approximate indexes (IVF, HNSW, DiskANN, ScaNN) skip most comparisons and lose a little recall; compression (PQ, int8, binary, shorter Matryoshka vectors) saves memory and also loses a little.
  • On our 1,076 chunks exact search is the right answer (see Touch).
  • Hybrid retrieval runs keyword and vector search and merges the lists (reciprocal rank fusion); a reranker (cross-encoder) then reorders the top few. Graph indexes (entities and their passages) add structure.
  • Metadata filters (only this book, chapter, lecture or the sources a class may use) must act before or during the search: filtering the results afterwards quietly loses chunks when the filter is selective (see Filters).
  • Our thesis choice: exact dense search plus BM25, fused with RRF, at the pilot scale; an approximate, compressed index only when the corpus grows (Level 3).
Level 0in one minute

Finding the right page in a big library

For anyone. No technical words.

A friend asks: "What does KKT stand for?" The answer is on one page among a thousand pages of lecture notes. You may hand over ten pages. How do you find them quickly?

Read every page

You never miss, but it takes the longest. Fine for a thousand pages, too slow for a million.

Look in the word list at the back

The list says on which pages "KKT" appears. Very fast for rare words, but it does not know that "a wide gap" and "a big margin" mean the same thing.

Shelves of similar pages

Pages about the same topic stand together. Walk to the two or three shelves closest to the question and read only those. Fast, but now and then the best page stands on a shelf you skipped.

Our 1,076 lecture chunks as dots (a flat picture of 1,024 numbers per chunk). Left: read every dot. Middle: the word list points straight at the few chunks that contain the word. Right: shelves (groups of similar chunks); only the nearest shelves are opened.

Takeaway: an index is a shortcut prepared before the question comes. Some shortcuts are exact (the word list finds every page with the word); others trade a small chance of a miss for a big gain in speed or space.
Level 1for a student

Twelve techniques, one corpus

For a student who knows what an embedding is: a list of numbers (here 1,024) that stands for the meaning of a text.

Retrieval has two steps. Offline, the system cuts the documents into chunks and builds an index. Online, it turns the question into the same form and asks the index for the top k chunks (here k = 10). Every technique below is a different answer to two questions: what do we store per chunk, and how much of the store must we touch per question? The numbers in the table come from our corpus.

Three pairs that people mix up

pair 1index recall vs. retrieval quality

The recall@10 of an approximate index on this page asks: of the 10 chunks that exact search returns, how many did the index also return? It measures what the shortcut loses, not whether the chunks answer the question. A perfect index on a weak embedding still returns the wrong chunks.

pair 2sparse vs. dense

A sparse vector has one slot per word of the vocabulary and almost all slots are zero (BM25, SPLADE, bge-m3 sparse). A dense vector has a few hundred to a few thousand slots and all are used. Sparse vectors live in an inverted index; dense vectors need a vector index.

pair 3first stage vs. second stage

An index (first stage) scores every chunk cheaply and returns a short list. A reranker (second stage) reads the question and each listed chunk together, which is far more accurate and far too slow to run on the whole corpus. It cannot find a chunk that the first stage missed.

Real indexes on 1,076 lecture chunks

Each setting below was built and measured on our corpus when this page was built (FAISS for the vector indexes, our BM25 for keywords; checked against the bm25s library). Pick a setting and the numbers and the picture change. Nothing is simulated: you browse a grid of real runs.

Recall against work

Every point is one real setting. x = distance computations per question (log scale; exact search = 1,076); y = recall@10 against exact search, averaged over 43 real questions. The filled ring is your current setting. Click a point to load it.

Recall against bytes per vector

One point per real setting: x = bytes stored per chunk vector (log scale; full 1,024 float32 numbers = 4,096 bytes); y = recall@10 against exact search on the full vectors. Rescoring = re-rank a longer compressed candidate list with the full vectors.

fuse:

Top 10 of each method over all 1,076 chunks: lecture, start of the 5-minute window and, when a window has several chunks, which one (·1, ·2, ...). Amber = a chunk that holds one of our answer quotes. Click a chunk to see its text and its rank in every list. RRF = sum over the fused lists of 1/(k + rank). Score fusion = weight × BM25 + (1 − weight) × dense, each rescaled to 0..1 over the candidate pool. The reranker (bge-reranker-v2-m3) scored the question against all 1,076 chunks here; in practice it would see only the first-stage top list.

Filterssearch inside a scope

Metadata filtering

For everyone who has seen a "search only in…" box. Plain words first, then the measurements, then our use.

Every chunk carries more than its text and its vector: metadata, small labels about where it comes from. A filter tells the retriever to search only chunks whose labels match. In a course tutor the useful labels are:

Where in the source

book, chapter, section, page or page range; course, lecture, time window of a video.

What kind of source

source type (book, lecture, paper, slide), language, licence (may we quote it?), version of the material.

Who may see it

the sources an administrator allows for a class or a tenant; exclusions, such as the exercise a question was made from.

The filter is a hard rule, not a preference: a chunk outside the scope must never reach the language model, however similar its vector is. The hard part is doing that and keeping the nearest-neighbour search fast and complete.

Three ways to combine a filter with vector search

pre-filterfilter first, then search the survivors

Select the chunks that pass, then search them exactly (or with an index built for that subset). Always complete; the cost grows with the number of survivors . Cheap for a selective filter, expensive for a broad one on a large corpus.

post-filtersearch first, then drop what fails

Ask the ordinary index for the top c candidates and drop the chunks that fail the filter. Fast, but with a selective filter few candidates survive, and the answer can be fewer than k chunks . pgvector works this way by default: with ef_search 40 and a filter that matches 10% of the rows, about 4 rows come back . Its iterative index scan keeps scanning until enough rows pass ; Neo4j post-filters with a plain WHERE but filters during the search with a WHERE inside SEARCH .

filtered ANNrespect the filter during the walk

The index itself knows the labels. Qdrant adds graph links per indexed payload value and lets a query planner choose between a full scan, the payload index and filterable HNSW by the estimated number of matches . Research indexes do the same with label-aware graphs: Filtered-DiskANN and ACORN, which reports 2 to 1,000 times higher throughput at fixed recall but still falls back to pre-filtering for very selective filters . LanceDB pre-filters by default .

Try it on our chunks: keep fewer and fewer lectures

x = share of the 1,076 chunks that pass the filter (k random lectures of 18, five random choices per k, averaged); y = recall@10 against exact search inside the filter, over 43 real questions. Pre-filter + exact search is complete by construction. Post-filter asks the HNSW index (M 16) for 10 or 100 candidates and drops the rest. The iterative scan doubles the candidate list until 10 pass (as pgvector's does). It keeps the index's own recall at small lists, so with no filter (100%) it falls back to plain HNSW with 10 candidates. "Inside the graph" is FAISS's filtered HNSW search (ef 64): it walks the whole graph and keeps only allowed chunks.

Three named filters

Partitions: one index per scope

When a filter is always the same kind (one tenant, one course, one language), the simplest fix is a separate index per value: each tenant or course gets its own small index and a query searches only its own. sqlite-vec calls this a partition key and needs hundreds of vectors per key value to pay off . A partition is a pre-filter decided at build time: complete and fast, but a query across scopes must search several indexes and merge them, and every new scope adds an index to build.

How we will use it

ours (planned design from the thesis pipeline proposal, not built yet)
  • Allowed sources per tenant. An administrator chooses the sources a class may use (which books, which lectures, which licences). The list becomes a pre-filter on every query; at our size exact search on the allowed chunks is cheap, so nothing outside the scope can be returned and nothing inside it is missed.
  • No leakage from exercises. A practice question made from an exercise carries derived_from (the exercise it came from). When that question is asked, the chunks of its own exercise and worked solution are excluded, so the tutor cannot copy the answer it was built from; results are reported with and without the exclusion. Worked solutions are kept out of the searchable passages altogether.
  • Citations by place. Every chunk keeps book, chapter, section and page (or lecture and time window), so the answer cites "book p. 58" or "Lecture 14, 00:10", and a student can narrow a search to one chapter.
  • Every arm, the same scope. One permitted-source list per evaluation condition applies to dense, sparse and BM25 search, to graph construction and graph summaries, and to agent tools, before fusion.
Takeaway: filter before or during the search, never only after it. Post-filtering an ordinary index quietly drops results when the filter is selective; on our chunks, keeping one lecture leaves less than one of ten chunks after post-filtering 10 candidates.
